entries.title: Bells: a world history

tiers.everyday: Bells have been made for about 3,000 years, from tiny Assyrian bronze bells to Chinese chime sets, Buddhist temple bells struck with a beam, European church and city bells, carillons played from a keyboard and giant Russian bells. Most are cast from bell bronze, about four parts copper to one part tin.
tiers.student: This overview links every bell in the Bells layer. It covers early bells (a Neo-Assyrian bell of 800–700 BC), the bianzhong of Marquis Yi of Zeng (5th century BCE), Buddhist bonshō and Korean bells, Christian church bells and medieval founding, Low Countries carillons, Russian giant bells, English change ringing, ship and civic bells and the modern era. It ends with how bells are cast in loam moulds from about 80% copper and 20% tin, then tuned by turning metal from the inside.

entries.summary: Bells have been made for about 3,000 years, from tiny Assyrian bronze bells to Chinese chime sets, Buddhist temple bells struck with a beam, European church and city bells, carillons played from a keyboard and giant Russian bells. entries.title: Tsar Bell

tiers.everyday: The Tsar Bell in the Moscow Kremlin is about 202 tonnes of bronze and has never been rung. It cracked in a fire in 1737 while still in its casting pit, and a huge piece broke off.
tiers.student: Cast in 1733–1735 by Ivan and Mikhail Motorin, the Tsar Bell (about 202 t, 6.14 m high, 6.6 m across) cracked during the Troitsky fire of May 1737, losing an 11.5 t fragment. It was raised onto a pedestal in 1836 and is a monument of Russian founding, never a working bell.

entries.title: Uglich alarm bell (the exiled bell)

tiers.everyday: In 1591 this bell rang the alarm in Uglich when the young Tsarevich Dmitry died. As punishment it was 'flogged', had its clapper torn out and was exiled to Siberia. It came home in 1892.
tiers.student: After the alarm of 15 May 1591, the bell was punished by decree of Boris Godunov (tongue torn out, ear cut off, 12 lashes) and exiled to Tobolsk. The Uglich museum records its return in May 1892, when it became a founding exhibit. Maker, mass and size [UNKNOWN].

entries.title: Big Ben (the Great Bell, Elizabeth Tower)

tiers.everyday: Big Ben is the nickname of the Great Bell in the Elizabeth Tower in London. It weighs 13.7 tonnes and strikes the note E. The first bell cracked, and the present one was recast at Whitechapel in 1858.
tiers.student: UK Parliament records: a first bell cast in August 1856 by Warners cracked in testing (October 1857); George Mears recast it at Whitechapel on 10 April 1858. It first struck on 11 July 1859, cracked that September, and from 1863 was turned 90° with a lighter (about 200 kg) hammer. 13.7 t, 2.7 m across, 2.2 m high, note E.

entries.title: Bow Bells (St Mary-le-Bow)

tiers.everyday: Bow Bells are the bells of St Mary-le-Bow in London. They were destroyed in the Great Fire of 1666 and again in a 1941 air raid, and the present twelve bells were first rung in 1961.
tiers.student: The church's history: lost in 1666; a peal of eight in 1677; tenor recast by Thomas Lester in 1738; twelve from 1881; recast by Gillett & Johnston in 1933; destroyed on 11 May 1941; recast at Whitechapel in 1956 using salvaged metal and first rung on 21 December 1961. A classic English change-ringing ring.

entries.title: Bianzhong of Marquis Yi of Zeng

tiers.everyday: These 65 bronze bells from the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng are about 2,400 years old. Each bell can play two different notes depending on where it is struck.
tiers.student: The Hubei Provincial Museum lists 65 bells (19 niuzhong, 45 yongzhong and one bo bell given by King Hui of Chu) on a 7.48 m rack in three tiers and eight groups, with 3,755 inscribed characters on music theory. Each bell sounds two tones a third apart; the set spans about 5.5 octaves. UNESCO lists it in Memory of the World.

tiers.student: The US Air Force records that the bells were used in a 1901 attack in which 45 US soldiers were killed, were kept at F.E. Warren AFB from 1904, joined the Air Force museum system in 1992 and were presented to the Philippines on 14 November 2018. Number of bells and present place [UNKNOWN] from official pages we could open.

entries.title: Liberty Bell

tiers.everyday: The Liberty Bell was made for the Pennsylvania State House (now Independence Hall). It weighs 2,080 lb and cracked for good in 1846. It became a symbol of freedom for abolitionists and many others.
tiers.student: NPS: ordered in 1751, first cast at Whitechapel (Lester & Pack) in 1752, cracked on test and recast twice by Pass and Stow in 1753. About 70% copper and 25% tin; 2,080 lb, 46.5 in across, 3 ft high. A thin crack was repaired in February 1846; it cracked again on 23 February 1846 and has not been rung since. NPS finds no evidence it rang on 4 or 8 July 1776; abolitionists named it the Liberty Bell in 1835.

entries.title: Wilbank Bell (Independence Hall, 1828)

tiers.everyday: The Wilbank Bell was cast in 1828 for the new tower of Independence Hall, between the Liberty Bell and the Centennial Bell. It later moved to Germantown.
tiers.student: NPS: John Wilbank cast a larger bell in 1828 for the rebuilt tower; listeners disliked its first ring on 4 July and he replaced it. The fact sheet gives 4,600 lb and 61.5 in. The bell went to Germantown Town Hall in 1877 and to its Germantown Avenue building in 1924.

entries.title: Centennial Bell (Independence Hall)

tiers.everyday: The Centennial Bell hangs where the Liberty Bell once did, in the Independence Hall tower. It weighs 13,000 lb and rings every hour.
tiers.student: NPS gives 13,000 lb and a 7 ft 6 in diameter, cast at Meneely-Kimberly in Troy in 1876. Its metal includes 400 lb from four cannons: one American and one British from Saratoga, one Union and one Confederate from Gettysburg (fact sheet). Since 1926 a hammer strikes it on the hour. The National Register form gives 7 ft 3/4 in across (conflict kept open).

entries.title: Justice Bell (Women's Liberty Bell)

tiers.everyday: The Justice Bell is a copy of the Liberty Bell made in 1915 for the fight for women's votes. Its clapper was chained so it could not ring until women won the vote in 1920.
tiers.student: NPS: commissioned in 1915 by Katharine Wentworth Ruschenberger of the Pennsylvania Woman Suffrage Association, cast by Meneely in Troy without a crack, inscribed 'ESTABLISH JUSTICE'. It toured Pennsylvania's 67 counties silent; after the 19th Amendment it was rung on 25 September 1920. A Library of Congress photo shows the casting.

entries.title: Bicentennial Bell (Philadelphia)

tiers.everyday: The Bicentennial Bell was a gift from the people of Britain for America's 200th birthday in 1976. It was cast at Whitechapel, the foundry that first cast the Liberty Bell.
tiers.student: NPS: cast at the Whitechapel Foundry, presented on 6 July 1976, inscribed 'LET FREEDOM RING'; 6 ft 10.5 in across and 5 ft 6 in high (2013 release), note G below middle C, 12,466 lb (the 2013 release says 12,446 lb). It rang from a tower on 3rd Street until moved to storage on 31 January 2013, and now stands in the Benjamin Rush Garden.

entries.title: Old North Church bells

tiers.everyday: The eight bells of Boston's Old North Church were cast in England in 1744. They were the first ring of change-ringing bells in North America.
tiers.student: The Boston Landmarks Commission records eight bells cast in 1744 by the Rudhall foundry of Gloucestershire and installed in 1745, more than 5,000 lb in all, the first change-ringing bells in the British American colonies; NPS calls them the nation's first maiden peal. Old North gives a 1,545 lb tenor; NPS notes that Paul Revere rang bells there as a teenager and that the 1775 lantern signal was shown from this bell tower. The NPS-archive tower report records rehanging in 1894.
